items.content: From 2000 to 2023, the cumulative mass loss of global glaciers (excluding the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets) amounted to -6542 ± 387 Gt. Glacial mass loss accelerated significantly over the obser
items.reasoning: Using Objective Evaluation (Mode A), the report accurately reproduces all key quantitative metrics from the original paper within uncertainties: cumulative 2000–2023 mass loss of -6605 ± 387 Gt (within 1% of -6542 ± 387 Gt), acceleration from -236 ± 22 Gt yr⁻¹ (2000–2011) to -315 ± 24 Gt yr⁻¹ (2012–2023) (+33 ± 16% vs. 36 ± 10%), and record 2023 mass loss of -569 ± 103 Gt (vs. -548 ± 120 Gt). It also substantiates that glaciers are the largest single land-ice contributor to sea-level rise, exceeding Greenland by 31% (1.31×) and Antarctica by nearly twofold (1.97×) over 2000–2018. However, it falls slightly short of the original paper because its calendar-year series relies on a linear weighting of hydrological years (36 Gt annual RMSD), its ice-sheet comparison uses an older 2000–2018 window rather than 2002–2021, and its main configuration was selected by benchmarking against the official results included in the dataset.

However, compared to the target figure's dual-panel CMIP5/CMIP6 continuous ensemble plumes and split 2000–2040/2040–2100 layout, the AI figure only draws linear interpolations from 2015 to 2100 point estimates and omits dual Gt/SLE axes. It also misses critical benchmarks, including observations surpassing the 2040 IPCC AR6 low-end projection, updated 2040 model ranges, regional model biases, and percentage offsets from earlier IPCC reports.
